newsitem.title: YEMEN: Yemen names independent economist as PM.
newsitem.headline: Yemen names independent economist as PM.

text.p: Yemeni President Ali Abdullah Saleh on Wednesday named Faraj Said Bin Ghanem, a Polish-educated economist, as prime minister, signalling a commitment to pursue market reforms.

State-run television said Saleh issued a decree asking Bin Ghanem, a former planning minister, to form a new government after Yemen's general elections last month in which the ruling General People's Party (GPC) won a majority in parliament.

Bin Ghanem replaces Abdul-Aziz Abdul-Ghani, a GPC member, who on Monday presented the government's resignation to Saleh following the April 27 polls, the first general elections since a 1994 civil war nearly tore the impoverished Arab state apart.
Officials said Bin Ghanem, in his late 50s and currently Yemen's ambassador to the European headquarters of the United Nations in Geneva, would form the government "soon".
A father of three, a daughter and two sons, Bin Ghanem hails from the southern province of Hadramaut. He became planning and development minister in 1990, in united Yemen's first government.
"The new cabinet is expected to include many new faces of mostly technocrats," one official said.
Bin Ghanem is expected to retain some former cabinet members, including Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Foreign Affairs Abdul-Karim al-Iryani, officials said.

Diplomats said Saleh's choice reflected his commitment to push ahead with tough economic reforms agreed with the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) to lure badly-needed foreign investments and trim budget deficits.
Some diplomats said they expected the new government to be in place before the first session of the newly-elected parliament on Sunday.
Yemen is one of the Arab world's poorest nations with a per capita GDP of $280 a year. Unemployment is around 25 percent.
A small independent oil producer, Yemen pumps around 385,000 barrels per day (bpd), of which 190,000 bpd come from the south.
Yemeni officials have said their economy is improving while central bank assets had risen with reforms introduced in 1995.
Saleh said last week his ruling GPC would run the country alone after it captured 187 seats in the 301-member parliament.
The Islah Party, GPC's Islamist junior coalition partner in the outgoing government, won 53 seats. It said it would join the opposition.
Independents won 54 seats and two opposition parties took a total of five seats. Results in two constituencies have yet to be announced.

In united Yemen's first elections in 1993, the GPC won 123, Islah 62, and the main opposition Yemen Socialist Party (YSP) 56. Independents won 47 seats while the rest went to Baathist and Nasserite parties.

The YSP, some of whose leaders launched a secessionist bid that sparked the civil war, and three other parties boycotted the elections to protest at alleged irregularities. The government denied the charges.
